figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Sliding Window Attention. The number of operations in vanilla attention is quadratic in the sequence length, and the memory increases linearly with the number of tokens. At inference time, this incurs higher latency and smaller throughput due to reduced cache availability. To alleviate this issue, we use sliding window attention: each token can attend to at most $W$ tokens from the previous layer (here, $W=3$). Note that tokens outside the sliding window still influence next word prediction. At each attention layer, information can move forward by $W$ tokens. Hence, after $k$ attention layers, information can move forward by up to $k\times W$ tokens.
figures.headline: Sliding window attention lets information move forward by up to k times W tokens after k layers, here with W set to 3.
citing_sentences: Recursively, $h_{i}$ can access tokens from the input layer at a distance of up to $W\times k$ tokens, as illustrated in Figure 1.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Rolling buffer cache. The cache has a fixed size of $W=4$. Keys and values for position $i$ are stored in position $i\bmod W$ of the cache. When the position $i$ is larger than $W$, past values in the cache are overwritten. The hidden state corresponding to the latest generated tokens are colored in orange.
figures.headline: A rolling cache of four slots overwrites old keys and values once positions exceed the window size.
citing_sentences: We provide an illustration in Figure 2 for $W=3$.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Pre-fill and chunking. During pre-fill of the cache, long sequences are chunked to limit memory usage. We process a sequence in three chunks, “The cat sat on”, “the mat and saw”, “the dog go to”. The figure shows what happens for the third chunk (“the dog go to”): it attends itself using a causal mask (rightmost block), attends the cache using a sliding window (center block), and does not attend to past tokens as they are outside of the sliding window (left block).
figures.headline: Pre-fill processes a long prompt in chunks, with each chunk attending to itself causally and to the cache through a sliding window.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 shows how the attention mask works over both the cache and the chunk.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Performance of Mistral 7B and different Llama models on a wide range of benchmarks. All models were re-evaluated on all metrics with our evaluation pipeline for accurate comparison. Mistral 7B significantly outperforms Llama 2 7B and Llama 2 13B on all benchmarks. It is also vastly superior to Llama 1 34B in mathematics, code generation, and reasoning benchmarks.
figures.headline: Mistral 7B exceeds Llama 2 7B and 13B on all benchmarks and Llama 1 34B in mathematics, code, and reasoning.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 compares the performance of Mistral 7B with Llama 2 7B/13B, and Llama 1 34B in different categories.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Results on MMLU, commonsense reasoning, world knowledge and reading comprehension for Mistral 7B and Llama 2 (7B/13B/70B). Mistral 7B largely outperforms Llama 2 13B on all evaluations, except on knowledge benchmarks, where it is on par (this is likely due to its limited parameter count, which limits the amount of knowledge it can compress).
figures.headline: Mistral 7B largely outperforms Llama 2 13B on MMLU, commonsense and reading tasks, but matches it on knowledge benchmarks.
citing_sentences: We computed “equivalent model sizes” of the Llama 2 family, aiming to understand Mistral 7B models’ efficiency in the cost-performance spectrum (see Figure 5).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Human evaluation of Mistral 7B – Instruct vs Llama 2 13B – Chat Example. An example of human evaluation from llmboxing.com. The question asks for recommendations of books in quantum physics. Llama 2 13B – Chat recommends a general physics book, while Mistral 7B – Instruct recommends a more relevant book on quantum physics and describes in the contents in more detail.
figures.headline: In one example, Mistral 7B – Instruct recommends a quantum physics book where Llama 2 13B – Chat recommends a general physics book.
citing_sentences: In this evaluation, participants were provided with a set of questions along with anonymous responses from two models and were asked to select their preferred response, as illustrated in Figure 6.

abstract: We introduce Mistral 7B, a 7–billion-parameter language model engineered for superior performance and efficiency. Mistral 7B outperforms the best open 13B model (Llama 2) across all evaluated benchmarks, and the best released 34B model (Llama 1) in reasoning, mathematics, and code generation. Our model leverages grouped-query attention (GQA) for faster inference, coupled with sliding window attention (SWA) to effectively handle sequences of arbitrary length with a reduced inference cost. We also provide a model fine-tuned to follow instructions, Mistral 7B – Instruct, that surpasses Llama 2 13B – chat model both on human and automated benchmarks. Our models are released under the Apache 2.0 license. Code: https://github.com/mistralai/mistral-src Webpage: https://mistral.ai/news/announcing-mistral-7b/

sections.body: The introduction presents Mistral 7B as a model designed for high performance with efficient inference. The authors state that it outperforms Llama 2 13B across all tested benchmarks and surpasses the best 34B model (LLaMa 34B) in mathematics and code generation. It approaches the coding performance of Code-Llama 7B without sacrificing performance on non-code benchmarks. The model uses grouped-query attention and sliding window attention, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license with a reference implementation for vLLM and Hugging Face. A chat model fine-tuned from it is said to significantly outperform Llama 2 13B – Chat.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Mistral 7B is a 7-billion-parameter open model that claims to beat Llama 2 13B on all tested benchmarks.

sections.body: The architecture changes Llama in three ways. In sliding window attention, each hidden state attends to the previous layer within a window of $W$ positions, so information reaches up to $W\times k$ tokens after $k$ layers. With $W=4096$, the theoretical attention span at the last layer is approximately 131K tokens. For a sequence length of 16K, the changes made to FlashAttention and xFormers give a 2x speed improvement over a vanilla attention baseline. A rolling buffer cache of fixed size $W$ overwrites old keys and values, reducing cache memory 8x on a 32k-token sequence without impacting model quality. Pre-fill and chunking process long prompts piece by piece to limit memory use.
sections.heading: Architectural details
sections.headline: Sliding window attention, a rolling buffer cache and chunked pre-fill reduce attention cost and cache memory.

sections.body: The authors re-run all benchmarks with their own evaluation pipeline, covering commonsense, world knowledge, reading comprehension, math, code, and aggregate tests such as MMLU and BBH. In Table 2, Mistral 7B scores 60.1% on MMLU against 55.6% for Llama 2 13B, and 52.2% on GSM8K against 34.3%. A size analysis finds that Mistral 7B matches a Llama 2 model more than 3x its size on reasoning and MMLU. On knowledge benchmarks the compression rate is only 1.9x, which the authors attribute to its limited parameter count. The MBPP results use the hand-verified subset, and TriviaQA is run without Wikipedia contexts, so comparisons with the Llama 2 paper are not exact.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Mistral 7B beats Llama 2 13B on all metrics and reaches 30.5% on HumanEval, near Code-Llama 7B's 31.1%.

sections.body: The instruct model was fine-tuned on publicly available Hugging Face instruction datasets, with no proprietary data or training tricks. On MT-Bench it is reported as superior to all 7B models and comparable to 13B chat models. An independent human evaluation on llmboxing.com asked participants to choose between anonymous responses from two models. As of October 6, 2023, Mistral 7B outputs were preferred 5020 times, compared with 4143 times for Llama 2 13B. The authors describe the fine-tuning as a simple and preliminary demonstration rather than an optimized model.
sections.heading: Instruction Finetuning
sections.headline: Mistral 7B – Instruct, tuned on public datasets, was preferred 5020 times over Llama 2 13B – Chat's 4143 times.

sections.body: The authors add a system prompt, similar to the one used for Llama 2, that steers answers within guardrails and lets users trade off utility against enforcement. On a set of 175 unsafe prompts, the model with the recommended prompt declines 100% of harmful questions. In one example about killing a Linux process, Mistral 7B – Instruct answers while Llama 2 13B – Chat declines, although both answer correctly when system prompts are off. For content moderation, a self-reflection prompt on a manually curated and balanced dataset of adversarial and standard prompts gives a precision of 99.4% and a recall of 95.6%, with acceptable prompts treated as positives.
sections.heading: Adding guardrails for front-facing applications
sections.headline: With a guardrail system prompt, Mistral 7B – Instruct declines 100% of 175 unsafe test prompts.

sections.body: The conclusion argues that language models may compress knowledge more than previously thought. The authors contend that scaling laws have so far been studied in 2 dimensions, relating capability to training cost, while the problem is 3 dimensional, also including inference cost. They state that much remains to be explored to find the best performance with the smallest possible model. The section gives no new experiments and offers this as a direction for future work.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Mistral 7B suggests models compress knowledge more than thought, so scaling laws must also weigh inference cost.
